1.meaning: Make people feel comfortable in a new situation
1.origin: From icebreaker ships clearing frozen waterways
1.example_daily: I told a joke to break the ice at the party.
1.example_interview: The interviewer broke the ice by asking about my hobbies.
1.example_corporate: Let's break the ice before we start the meeting.

1.meaning: To endure a painful or otherwise unpleasant situation that is seen as unavoidable
1.origin: From the historical practice of having a patient bite on a bullet during surgery without anesthesia
1.example_daily: I have to bite the bullet and go to the dentist.
1.example_interview: I decided to bite the bullet and apply for the senior role.
1.example_corporate: We need to bite the bullet and cut the budget.

1.meaning: To do something badly or cheaply to save time or money
1.origin: Likely from taking a shortcut by literally cutting across a corner
1.example_daily: Don't cut corners when painting the house.
1.example_interview: I never cut corners when it comes to code quality.
1.example_corporate: Cutting corners on safety is unacceptable.

1.origin: From horseback riding, where the reins slip out of the rider's hand
1.example_daily: The party got out of hand.
1.example_interview: I implemented a new system before the technical debt got out of hand.
1.example_corporate: Project scope creep is getting out of hand.

1.origin: From an iconic 1970s poster featuring a cat clinging to a branch
1.example_daily: Hang in there, the weekend is almost here.
1.example_interview: I learned to hang in there when solving complex bugs.
1.example_corporate: We need to hang in there until the merger is complete.

1.origin: From arriving at the dock after the boat has departed
1.example_daily: I missed the boat on buying those concert tickets.
1.example_interview: I don't want to miss the boat on AI technology.
1.example_corporate: If we don't launch soon, we'll miss the boat.

1.meaning: You have to work for what you want
1.origin: A proverb dating back to the second century
1.example_daily: My legs ache from the gym, but no pain, no gain.
1.example_interview: Learning that framework was tough, but no pain, no gain.
1.example_corporate: The restructuring will be difficult, but no pain, no gain.

1.meaning: Doing a good job, being quick to understand
1.origin: From sports, keeping your eye on the ball
1.example_daily: She's really on the ball today.
1.example_interview: I make sure to stay on the ball with industry trends.
1.example_corporate: We need a manager who is on the ball.

1.origin: Possibly from the 18th century street thieves who tripped their victims
1.example_interview: I thought he was pulling my leg when he offered me the job.
1.example_corporate: I was just pulling your leg about the weekend work.

1.origin: Modern idiom from the idea of physically embracing a concept
1.example_daily: I can't wrap my head around this math problem.
1.example_interview: It took me a while to wrap my head around the legacy codebase.
1.example_corporate: We need to wrap our heads around the new regulations.

2.meaning: A good thing that seemed bad at first
2.origin: Mid-18th century poem by James Hervey
2.example_daily: Losing my job was a blessing in disguise.
2.example_interview: That failed project was a blessing in disguise as it taught me a lot.
2.example_corporate: The delayed launch might be a blessing in disguise.

2.origin: From the 19th century when goods were sold by the dozen
2.example_daily: Those vintage shirts are a dime a dozen.
2.example_interview: Basic coding skills are a dime a dozen; problem-solving is rare.
2.example_corporate: Consultants like that are a dime a dozen.

2.meaning: Avoid saying what you mean, usually because it is uncomfortable
2.origin: From bird hunting, beating bushes to flush out birds
2.example_daily: Stop beating around the bush and tell me the truth.
2.example_interview: I prefer direct communication rather than beating around the bush.
2.example_corporate: Let's not beat around the bush; the Q3 numbers are bad.

2.meaning: Better to arrive late than not to come at all
2.origin: Traced back to Geoffrey Chaucer's 'The Canterbury Tales'
2.example_daily: He finally finished the report. Better late than never.
2.example_interview: I started my tech career later in life, but better late than never.
2.example_corporate: The update is delayed, but better late than never.

2.origin: From the phrase 'call it a half-day' in the mid-19th century
2.example_daily: I'm tired, let's call it a day.
2.example_interview: I don't call it a day until my code compiles successfully.
2.example_corporate: It's 6 PM, let's call it a day.

2.idiom: Give someone the benefit of the doubt
2.example_daily: I'll give him the benefit of the doubt this time.
2.example_interview: I try to give my teammates the benefit of the doubt.
2.example_corporate: We should give the vendor the benefit of the doubt regarding the delay.

2.origin: From WWII era when mattresses were often sacks filled with hay
2.example_daily: I'm exhausted, time to hit the sack.
2.example_interview: I ensure I hit the sack early before a big release.
2.example_corporate: After this long flight, I just want to hit the sack.

2.origin: Emerged in America during the 1980s space program
2.example_daily: Just plug it in, it's not rocket science.
2.example_interview: Learning HTML isn't rocket science, but mastering it takes time.
2.example_corporate: Fixing this process is not rocket science.

2.example_daily: To make a long story short, we broke up.
2.example_interview: To make a long story short, I led the migration to AWS.
2.example_corporate: Make a long story short: did we get the contract?

2.meaning: Things are going well so far
2.origin: First recorded in a 1718 Scottish proverb collection
2.example_daily: How is the new house? So far so good.
2.example_interview: My transition to the new framework has been so far so good.
2.example_corporate: Phase one is complete. So far so good.

3.origin: Nautical origin, sailors going below deck when ill
3.example_daily: I'm feeling a bit under the weather.
3.example_interview: Even when under the weather, I ensure my tasks are delegated.
3.example_corporate: The CEO is under the weather and will miss the meeting.

3.example_daily: It's hot today. You can say that again!
3.example_interview: Tech is moving fast. You can say that again.
3.example_corporate: This merger is stressful. You can say that again.

3.idiom: Your guess is as good as mine
3.example_daily: What time does the bus arrive? Your guess is as good as mine.
3.example_interview: When will the legacy system be retired? Your guess is as good as mine.
3.example_corporate: How the market will react is anyone's guess.

3.idiom: A bird in the hand is worth two in the bush
3.meaning: What you have is worth more than what you might have later
3.example_daily: I'll take this offer; a bird in the hand.
3.example_interview: I focus on delivering MVP first; a bird in the hand is worth two in the bush.
3.example_corporate: Let's secure this client now rather than wait for a bigger one.

3.origin: Coined by Sir Thomas More in 1522
3.example_daily: You look sad, a penny for your thoughts?
3.example_interview: A penny for your thoughts on this new architecture.
3.example_corporate: We need fresh ideas; a penny for your thoughts, team.

3.origin: Used in advertising in the early 1900s
3.example_daily: Look at this photo; a picture is worth a thousand words.
3.example_interview: I prefer using flowcharts because a picture is worth 1000 words.
3.example_corporate: Include a graph in the report, a picture is worth a thousand words.

3.meaning: Believe what people do and not what they say
3.example_daily: He said he'd help, but actions speak louder than words.
3.example_interview: I can list my skills, but my GitHub shows that actions speak louder.
3.example_corporate: Our commitment to diversity must be shown through action.

3.meaning: To make a bad situation worse
3.example_daily: My car broke down, and to add insult to injury, it started raining.
3.example_interview: The server crashed, and to add insult to injury, the backup failed.
3.example_corporate: Losing the client added insult to injury after a bad quarter.

3.meaning: To be mistaken, to be looking for solutions in the wrong place
3.origin: From hunting dogs barking at the wrong tree after prey has escaped
3.example_daily: If you think I broke it, you're barking up the wrong tree.
3.example_interview: I realized we were barking up the wrong tree with that database schema.
3.example_corporate: The marketing team is barking up the wrong tree with this demographic.

3.idiom: Bite off more than you can chew
3.meaning: Take on a project that you cannot finish
3.example_daily: I bit off more than I could chew by taking three classes.
3.example_interview: I learned early in my career not to bite off more than I can chew.
3.example_corporate: We bit off more than we could chew with the Q2 roadmap.

4.idiom: By the skin of your teeth
4.origin: From the Book of Job in the Bible
4.example_daily: I caught the train by the skin of my teeth.
4.example_interview: We met the deployment deadline by the skin of our teeth.
4.example_corporate: The company avoided bankruptcy by the skin of its teeth.

4.meaning: There's no reason to complain about something that can't be fixed
4.origin: An old proverb dating back to the 17th century
4.example_daily: I broke the glass, but don't cry over spilt milk.
4.example_interview: When a bug goes to production, I fix it rather than cry over spilt milk.
4.example_corporate: We lost the bid, but there's no use crying over spilt milk.

4.idiom: Don't put all your eggs in one basket
4.meaning: What you're doing is too risky
4.origin: From Don Quixote by Miguel de Cervantes
4.example_daily: Apply to multiple colleges; don't put all your eggs in one basket.
4.example_interview: I learned multiple programming languages so I wouldn't put all my eggs in one basket.
4.example_corporate: Diversify our investments; don't put all your eggs in one basket.

4.idiom: Every cloud has a silver lining
4.meaning: Good things come after bad things
4.example_daily: I lost my phone, but I got a better one. Every cloud has a silver lining.
4.example_interview: The project failure taught us a lot; every cloud has a silver lining.
4.example_corporate: The market crash led to better regulations; every cloud has a silver lining.

4.idiom: Get a taste of your own medicine
4.meaning: Get treated the way you've been treating others
4.example_daily: He finally got a taste of his own medicine.
4.example_interview: I learned empathy when I got a taste of my own medicine in a difficult review.
4.example_corporate: The aggressive competitor got a taste of its own medicine.

4.origin: Possibly from serving unwanted guests cold meat
4.example_daily: She gave me the cold shoulder at the party.
4.example_interview: I never give junior devs the cold shoulder when they ask for help.
4.example_corporate: The investors gave us the cold shoulder.

4.idiom: Go on a wild goose chase
4.origin: Used by Shakespeare in Romeo and Juliet
4.example_daily: Looking for my keys was a wild goose chase.
4.example_interview: Debugging without logs is a wild goose chase.
4.example_corporate: This investigation is a wild goose chase.

4.origin: From a poem by Thomas Gray
4.example_daily: I didn't know what was in the hot dog; ignorance is bliss.
4.example_interview: Sometimes concerning legacy code, ignorance is bliss.
4.example_corporate: When it comes to office politics, ignorance is bliss.

4.example_daily: I left no stone unturned looking for my wallet.
4.example_interview: When resolving a critical outage, I leave no stone unturned.
4.example_corporate: The auditors left no stone unturned.

4.idiom: Let the cat out of the bag
4.origin: From the scam of selling a cat instead of a pig in a bag
4.example_daily: Who let the cat out of the bag about the surprise party?
4.example_interview: I accidentally let the cat out of the bag about the new feature.
4.example_corporate: The press release let the cat out of the bag early.

5.origin: Literally sitting on a fence between two properties
5.example_daily: I'm on the fence about which movie to watch.
5.example_interview: I was on the fence between React and Angular, but chose React.
5.example_corporate: The board is still on the fence regarding the acquisition.

5.origin: From the rare occurrence of two full moons in one month
5.example_daily: I eat fast food once in a blue moon.
5.example_interview: Server crashes like that only happen once in a blue moon.
5.example_corporate: The CEO visits this office once in a blue moon.

5.meaning: A job, task or other activity that is easy or simple
5.origin: From the 1930s, likely related to the cakewalk dance
5.example_daily: That test was a piece of cake.
5.example_interview: Setting up the development environment was a piece of cake.
5.example_corporate: The integration should be a piece of cake.

5.origin: To physically bring oneself into an upright, composed posture
5.example_daily: You need to pull yourself together before the exam.
5.example_interview: I took a deep breath to pull myself together before the interview.
5.example_corporate: The team needs to pull itself together after the failed launch.

5.example_daily: I'm saving this bonus for a rainy day.
5.example_interview: I like to optimize resources and save compute power for a rainy day.
5.example_corporate: We need strong cash reserves to save for a rainy day.

5.meaning: The person we were just talking about showed up
5.origin: From the phrase 'Speak of the devil and he will appear'
5.example_daily: Speak of the devil, here comes John.
5.example_interview: We were just discussing the database, and speak of the devil, the DBA joined the call.
5.example_corporate: Speak of the devil, the client just emailed.

5.meaning: Take credit for someone else's work
5.origin: From playwright John Dennis whose thunder machine was copied
5.example_daily: She wore white to the wedding to steal the bride's thunder.
5.example_interview: I always credit my team and never steal their thunder.
5.example_corporate: The competitor launched their product early to steal our thunder.

5.idiom: Take it with a grain of salt
5.origin: From the Roman idea that poison is more easily swallowed with salt
5.example_daily: Take his advice with a grain of salt.
5.example_interview: I take online tutorials with a grain of salt and read the official docs.
5.example_corporate: Take these early sales projections with a grain of salt.

5.example_daily: Working from home offers the best of both worlds.
5.example_interview: Using TypeScript gives us the best of both worlds: JavaScript flexibility and type safety.
5.example_corporate: This hybrid approach gives us the best of both worlds.

5.meaning: The big issue, the problem people are avoiding
5.origin: First used in 1959 by The New York Times
5.example_daily: Let's address the elephant in the room: who broke the vase?
5.example_interview: I brought up the elephant in the room: our mounting technical debt.
5.example_corporate: We need to discuss the elephant in the room: budget cuts.

6.example_daily: Let's throw caution to the wind and go on a road trip.
6.example_interview: I don't usually throw caution to the wind when deploying to production.
6.example_corporate: The company threw caution to the wind with this aggressive expansion.

6.example_interview: I automate repetitive tasks because time is money.
6.example_corporate: We must streamline operations; time is money.

6.origin: From the phrase 'water under the bridge'
6.example_daily: We fought, but it's water under the bridge now.
6.example_interview: My initial struggles with Git are water under the bridge.
6.example_corporate: The previous dispute with the vendor is water under the bridge.

6.origin: From the days of oil lamps
6.example_daily: I have to burn the midnight oil to finish this essay.
6.example_interview: I'm willing to burn the midnight oil to ensure a successful release.
6.example_corporate: The legal team is burning the midnight oil on this contract.

6.origin: Refers to playing games by the rulebook
6.example_daily: He does everything by the book.
6.example_interview: I follow coding standards and do things by the book.
6.example_corporate: The compliance audit requires us to do everything by the book.

6.example_daily: Enough chatting, let's get down to business.
6.example_interview: After introductions, the interviewer got down to business.
6.example_corporate: Let's review the agenda and get down to business.

6.origin: From the Bible, Sermon on the Mount
6.example_daily: She always goes the extra mile for her friends.
6.example_interview: I always go the extra mile to write comprehensive unit tests.
6.example_corporate: Our customer service team is trained to go the extra mile.

6.origin: From Pliny the Elder who claimed a copy of the Iliad could fit in a nutshell
6.example_daily: In a nutshell, it was a terrible movie.
6.example_interview: In a nutshell, my role was to optimize the backend API.
6.example_corporate: In a nutshell, we need to increase revenue by 10%.

6.idiom: Keep your eye on the prize
6.origin: From a folk song popularized during the Civil Rights Movement
6.example_daily: Studying is hard, but keep your eye on the prize.
6.example_interview: During long sprints, I keep my eye on the prize of a stable product.
6.example_corporate: We have setbacks, but let's keep our eye on the prize: market dominance.

6.meaning: Learn how to do a job
6.origin: From sailing, learning how to handle the ropes on a ship
6.example_daily: It takes time to learn the ropes at a new school.
6.example_interview: It took me a month to learn the ropes of the new tech stack.
6.example_corporate: The new hires are still learning the ropes.

7.origin: From reading from the same page in a book
7.example_daily: Are we on the same page about dinner plans?
7.example_interview: I have daily standups to ensure the whole team is on the same page.
7.example_corporate: Before we sign, let's make sure we are all on the same page.

7.origin: From brewers testing the temperature of beer with their thumb
7.example_daily: As a rule of thumb, I drink two liters of water a day.
7.example_interview: A good rule of thumb is to keep functions small and focused.
7.example_corporate: Our rule of thumb is to respond to clients within 24 hours.

7.example_daily: My sister and I don't see eye to eye.
7.example_interview: Even if we don't see eye to eye, I can respectfully compromise.
7.example_corporate: Management and the union finally see eye to eye.

7.origin: Military term for holding a position
7.example_daily: He stood his ground during the argument.
7.example_interview: I stood my ground on using the more secure encryption method.
7.example_corporate: The negotiator stood his ground on the price.

7.idiom: Take the bull by the horns
7.origin: From the American West, wrestling steers
7.example_daily: I need to take the bull by the horns and clean my room.
7.example_interview: I took the bull by the horns and refactored the legacy module myself.
7.example_corporate: The CEO took the bull by the horns to solve the PR crisis.

7.example_daily: We need to think outside the box for this art project.
7.example_interview: I think outside the box when designing scalable architectures.
7.example_corporate: The marketing campaign requires us to think outside the box.

7.origin: From baseball, touching a base to be safe
7.example_daily: I'll touch base with you tomorrow.
7.example_interview: I like to touch base with product managers weekly.
7.example_corporate: Let's touch base after the conference.

7.origin: From a coin toss before it lands
7.example_daily: Our vacation plans are still up in the air.
7.example_interview: The choice of database was up in the air until we ran benchmarks.
7.example_corporate: The Q4 budget is still up in the air.

7.example_daily: I heard about the restaurant through word of mouth.
7.example_interview: Many open-source tools gain popularity through word of mouth.
7.example_corporate: Word of mouth marketing is our biggest growth driver.

7.idiom: At the end of the day
7.example_daily: At the end of the day, family is what matters most.
7.example_interview: At the end of the day, delivering value to the user is key.
7.example_corporate: At the end of the day, the bottom line is profit.
